manifest.policy: Every statement is a claim with at least one reference (url, retrieval date). Claims paraphrase pages and abstracts retrieved on the stated date; they are not independent measurements. Status: observed, inferred, hypothesis (including open questions) or historical.

notes.oneLine: The Solar System's star: a ball of hydrogen and helium about 4.5 billion years old.

what.text: The Sun is the only star in the Solar System, a ball of hydrogen and helium held together by its own gravity.

references.label: NASA Science: Sun Facts

what.text: It is about 100 times wider than Earth (NASA's rounded figure; the atlas radius of 695,700 km is about 109 Earth radii) and more than 330,000 Earths would be needed to match its mass.

references.label: NASA Science: Sun Facts

what.text: It is about 4.5 billion years old and NASA says it is a little less than halfway through its lifetime.

references.label: NASA Science: Sun Facts

why.text: Nuclear reactions that fuse hydrogen into helium power the Sun's heat and light.

references.label: NASA Science: Sun Facts

why.text: The temperature in the Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius.

references.label: NASA Science: Sun Facts

interesting.text: Roughly every 11 years the Sun's magnetic poles swap polarity; the peak of the activity cycle (solar maximum) brings many more solar storms.

references.label: NASA Science: Sun Facts

uncertain.text: Whether the corona is much hotter than the visible surface, and how the solar wind accelerates, are open questions that Parker Solar Probe was designed to address.

references.label: NASA Science: Parker Solar Probe

studiedBy.role: Launched 12 Aug 2018 to study the Sun's corona and solar wind from close range.

notes.oneLine: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun; one solar day lasts 176 Earth days.

what.text: Mercury is the smallest planet in the Solar System and the nearest to the Sun, with a radius of 2,440 km (atlas mean radius 2,439.4 km).

references.label: NASA Science: Mercury Facts

what.text: It orbits the Sun every 88 days, and one solar day (a full day-night cycle) lasts 176 Earth days.

references.label: NASA Science: Mercury Facts

why.text: With no atmosphere to retain heat, only a thin exosphere of atoms blasted off the surface, its surface temperature ranges from about 430 degrees Celsius by day to about minus 180 degrees Celsius at night.

references.label: NASA Science: Mercury Facts

interesting.text: MESSENGER found evidence of past volcanic activity and a significant northward offset of Mercury's magnetic field from the planet's centre.

references.label: NASA Science: MESSENGER

uncertain.text: NASA says Mercury may have water ice at its poles inside deep craters that stay in permanent shadow.

references.label: NASA Science: Mercury Facts

uncertain.text: MESSENGER found evidence of water ice at Mercury's poles, in places that never see sunlight; this is evidence from remote measurements, not a sample.

references.label: NASA Science: MESSENGER

studiedBy.role: Entered orbit around Mercury on 18 March 2011 and ended its mission by impact on 30 April 2015, after taking nearly 100,000 images.

notes.oneLine: Earth's size twin with a carbon-dioxide atmosphere, a surface near 467 C, and a slow backwards spin.

what.text: Venus is about 12,104 km across at the equator, compared with 12,756 km for Earth.

references.label: NASA Science: Venus Facts

what.text: Its atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, with dense clouds of sulfuric acid.

references.label: NASA Science: Venus Facts

why.text: Surface temperature is about 467 degrees Celsius and surface pressure is 93 times that at sea level on Earth.

references.label: NASA Science: Venus Facts

why.text: Venus spins slowly in the opposite direction from most planets; NASA gives 243 Earth days for its day length.

references.label: NASA Science: Venus Facts

interesting.text: Magellan found that at least 85% of the surface is covered with volcanic flows, and that continental drift is not evident.

references.label: NASA Science: Magellan

uncertain.text: NASA's page describes Venus and Earth as both having had oceans in their younger days, with Venus's now vanished; the page gives no amount or duration, so this is an inference about the past.

references.label: NASA Science: Venus Facts

studiedBy.role: Radar-mapped the surface; by Sept 1992 it had covered 98% of Venus.
Soviet probes sent to Venus between 1961 and 1984.

notes.oneLine: Our home planet: 71% ocean, a nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere, and the only planet with liquid water on its surface.

what.text: Earth is about 12,756 km across at the equator, the biggest of the terrestrial planets.

references.label: NASA Science: Earth Facts

what.text: Near the surface its atmosphere is 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% other gases.

references.label: NASA Science: Earth Facts

why.text: A global ocean covers about 71% of the surface, and Earth is the only planet in the Solar System with liquid water on the surface.

references.label: NASA Science: Earth Facts

interesting.text: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, when the Solar System settled into its current layout; its rapid rotation and molten nickel-iron core give rise to its magnetic field.

references.label: NASA Science: Earth Facts

uncertain.text: NASA dates the start of life to 'about 3.8 billion years ago'; this is an estimate, and the page does not describe how life began.

references.label: NASA Science: Earth Facts

studiedBy.role: Many orbiting spacecraft study Earth from above as a whole system.

notes.oneLine: Earth's Moon: tidally locked, heavily cratered, and likely formed from a giant impact.

what.text: The Moon has a radius of about 1,740 km (atlas: 1,737.53 km), less than a third of Earth's width, at an average distance of 384,400 km.

references.label: NASA Science: Moon Facts

what.text: Its solid rocky surface is cratered and pitted by impacts of asteroids, meteorites and comets.

references.label: NASA Science: Moon Facts

why.text: Earth and the Moon are tidally locked, so the same hemisphere always faces Earth.

references.label: NASA Science: Moon Facts

interesting.text: There are high concentrations of water ice in the permanently shadowed regions of the lunar poles.

references.label: NASA Science: Moon Facts

interesting.text: Apollo astronauts returned 842 pounds (382 kilograms) of lunar rock and soil to Earth.

references.label: NASA Science: Moon Facts

uncertain.text: NASA says the Moon likely formed after a Mars-sized body collided with Earth several billion years ago; 'likely' marks this as a leading hypothesis rather than a settled fact.

references.label: NASA Science: Moon Facts

studiedBy.role: Astronauts brought back 382 kg of lunar rocks and soil.
Launched 18 June 2009; maps the surface and helps identify areas near the south pole with water and extended sunlight.

notes.oneLine: A cold, thin-aired world with ancient river valleys and Olympus Mons, the largest volcano in the Solar System.

what.text: Mars has a radius of about 3,390 km, about half the size of Earth.

references.label: NASA Science: Mars Facts

what.text: Its thin atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, nitrogen and argon, and it has seasons and polar ice caps.

references.label: NASA Science: Mars Facts

why.text: Mars appears to have had a watery past, with ancient river valley networks, deltas and lakebeds.

references.label: NASA Science: Mars Facts

interesting.text: Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in the Solar System, and the Valles Marineris canyon system is long enough to stretch from California to New York.

references.label: NASA Science: Mars Facts

uncertain.text: Its two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, may be captured asteroids; the wording is NASA's, so their origin is not settled.

references.label: NASA Science: Mars Facts

uncertain.text: NASA says scientists do not expect to find living things currently thriving on Mars.

references.label: NASA Science: Mars Facts

studiedBy.role: Mars is the only planet where rovers have been sent to roam the surface.
High-resolution imaging, including of Phobos.

notes.oneLine: The largest planet, mostly hydrogen and helium, with a storm bigger than Earth that has raged for centuries.

what.text: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System; if it were a hollow shell, 1,000 Earths could fit inside.

references.label: NASA Science: Jupiter Facts

what.text: Its composition is similar to the Sun's: mostly hydrogen and helium.

references.label: NASA Science: Jupiter Facts

why.text: The Great Red Spot is a giant storm bigger than Earth that has raged for hundreds of years.

references.label: NASA Science: Jupiter Facts

discovery.text: Jupiter's four largest moons were first observed by Galileo Galilei in 1610 with an early telescope.

references.label: NASA Science: Jupiter Facts

discovery.text: Jupiter's rings were discovered in 1979 by Voyager 1.

references.label: NASA Science: Jupiter Facts

interesting.text: Jupiter's magnetic field is 16 to 54 times as powerful as Earth's, and the IAU officially recognises 115 moons (NASA's count at retrieval).

references.label: NASA Science: Jupiter Facts

uncertain.text: Juno's gravity and magnetic-field data suggest the core is much larger than expected and partially dissolved, with no clear boundary to the metallic hydrogen around it; this is inferred from measurements made from orbit.

references.label: NASA Science: Jupiter Facts
NASA Science: Juno

studiedBy.role: Orbited Jupiter from December 1995 until it was deliberately sent into Jupiter on 21 Sept 2003; first to measure the atmosphere directly with a descent probe.
In orbit since 4 July 2016 to learn Jupiter's origin and evolution, interior and magnetosphere.

notes.oneLine: A hydrogen-helium giant less dense than water, circled by rings of ice and rock chunks.

what.text: Saturn has an equatorial diameter of about 120,500 km, nine times wider than Earth, and is made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

references.label: NASA Science: Saturn Facts

what.text: It is the only planet whose average density is less than water (atlas: 0.687 g/cm3).

references.label: NASA Science: Saturn Facts

why.text: Its rings are billions of small chunks of ice and rock coated with other materials such as dust.

references.label: NASA Science: Saturn Facts

interesting.text: Saturn's north pole has a six-sided jet stream, first noticed in Voyager images in the early 1980s; NASA counted 274 confirmed moons in March 2025.

references.label: NASA Science: Saturn Facts

uncertain.text: Saturn's rings are thought to be pieces of comets, asteroids or shattered moons; their origin is uncertain.

references.label: NASA Science: Saturn Facts

studiedBy.role: First spacecraft to orbit Saturn; arrived 2004 and ended on 15 Sept 2017.
First noticed the six-sided jet stream at the north pole in the early 1980s.

notes.oneLine: An ice giant tipped on its side (97.77 degree tilt), found by William Herschel in 1781.

what.text: Uranus has an equatorial diameter of about 51,118 km, four times wider than Earth (atlas mean radius 25,362 km), and is one of two ice giants.

references.label: NASA Science: Uranus Facts

what.text: It is mostly swirling fluids and has two sets of rings and 28 known moons.

references.label: NASA Science: Uranus Facts

why.text: Its equator is nearly at a right angle to its orbit, with a tilt of 97.77 degrees.

references.label: NASA Science: Uranus Facts

discovery.text: Uranus was discovered in 1781 by William Herschel, who first thought it a comet or star; it was the first planet found with the aid of a telescope.

references.label: NASA Science: Uranus Facts

uncertain.text: NASA says the composition of Uranus's outer moons remains unknown, though they are likely captured asteroids.

references.label: NASA Science: Uranus Facts

studiedBy.role: The first human-made object to fly past Uranus (1986), and still the only spacecraft to have visited it.

notes.oneLine: The first planet located by mathematical prediction (1846), with winds up to three times Jupiter's.

what.text: Neptune has an equatorial diameter of about 49,528 km, about four times wider than Earth, and an atmosphere mostly of hydrogen and helium with a little methane.

references.label: NASA Science: Neptune Facts

what.text: It has 16 known moons.

references.label: NASA Science: Neptune Facts

why.text: Neptune's winds can be three times stronger than Jupiter's and nine times stronger than Earth's.

references.label: NASA Science: Neptune Facts

discovery.text: Neptune was found in 1846 and was the first planet located through mathematical predictions; Urbain Le Verrier had proposed the position and mass of the then-unknown planet.

references.label: NASA Science: Neptune Facts

interesting.text: The Great Dark Spot was large enough to contain the entire Earth.

references.label: NASA Science: Neptune Facts

uncertain.text: Scientists think there might be an ocean of super-hot water under Neptune's cold clouds; this is a proposal, not an observation.

references.label: NASA Science: Neptune Facts

studiedBy.role: The first human-made object to fly by Neptune, in August 1989; no other spacecraft has visited.

notes.oneLine: The most volcanically active world in the Solar System, with hundreds of volcanoes.

what.text: Io is only slightly larger than Earth's Moon and about one-quarter the diameter of Earth.

references.label: NASA Science: Io

what.text: It has hundreds of volcanoes, some erupting lava fountains dozens of miles high, and lakes of molten silicate lava.

references.label: NASA Science: Io

why.text: Io is caught in a tug-of-war between Jupiter's gravity and the precisely timed pulls of two neighbouring moons, which NASA presents as the driver of its volcanism.

references.label: NASA Science: Io

discovery.text: Galileo Galilei discovered Io and Jupiter's three other largest moons in 1610.

references.label: NASA Science: Callisto

discovery.text: Voyager 1 spotted the first signs of Io's powerful volcanism in 1979.

references.label: NASA Science: Io

uncertain.text: Galileo results indicate Io's volcanic activity may be 100 times greater than Earth's; the 'may' marks this as an estimate.

references.label: NASA Science: Galileo

studiedBy.role: Spotted the first signs of Io's powerful volcanism in 1979.
Source of most of what is known about Io.
Came within roughly 1,500 km of Io's surface on its 57th and 58th orbits.

notes.oneLine: An icy moon of Jupiter with strong evidence for a saltwater ocean beneath its ice.

what.text: Europa is the fourth largest of Jupiter's moons.

references.label: NASA Science: Europa

what.text: Most of what is known about the moon comes from observations by the Galileo mission.

references.label: NASA Science: Europa

why.text: NASA says there is strong evidence that Europa has a saltwater ocean; the Galileo mission page calls it a theory supported by evidence, so the ocean is inferred, not directly sampled.

references.label: NASA Science: Europa Clipper
NASA Science: Galileo

discovery.text: Galileo Galilei discovered Europa and Jupiter's three other largest moons in 1610.

references.label: NASA Science: Callisto

uncertain.text: Whether there are places below Europa's surface that could support life is the question Europa Clipper was built to investigate; it is not answered yet.

references.label: NASA Science: Europa Clipper

studiedBy.role: Orbited Jupiter 1995-2003 and made close passes of its major moons; main source of Europa data.
Launched 14 Oct 2024; due to reach Jupiter in April 2030.
Planned a rendezvous with Europa in September 2022.

notes.oneLine: NASA calls Ganymede the largest moon in the Solar System and the only one with its own magnetic field.

what.text: NASA describes Ganymede as the largest moon in the Solar System.

references.label: NASA Science: Ganymede

what.text: It is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field, which NASA attributes to a metallic iron core deep inside.

references.label: NASA Science: Ganymede

why.text: The magnetic field causes auroras, bright ribbons of glowing gas that circle the moon's poles.

references.label: NASA Science: Ganymede

discovery.text: Galileo Galilei discovered Ganymede and Jupiter's three other largest moons in 1610.

references.label: NASA Science: Callisto

uncertain.text: NASA calls the evidence for an underground saltwater ocean 'strong'; the ocean itself has not been observed directly.

references.label: NASA Science: Ganymede

uncertain.text: There is evidence that Ganymede has a tenuous oxygen atmosphere.

references.label: NASA Science: Ganymede

studiedBy.role: First close encounter with Ganymede on 26 June 1996.
Close flyby on 7 June 2021, with detailed photographs.

notes.oneLine: Jupiter's second largest moon, called the most heavily cratered object in the Solar System by NASA.

what.text: Callisto is Jupiter's second largest moon and the third largest moon in the Solar System.

references.label: NASA Science: Callisto

why.text: NASA calls Callisto the most heavily cratered object in the Solar System.

references.label: NASA Science: Callisto

discovery.text: Callisto and Jupiter's three other largest moons were discovered in 1610 by Galileo Galilei.

references.label: NASA Science: Callisto

uncertain.text: Galileo data from the 1990s suggest Callisto may have a salty ocean beneath its surface; this is less certain than for Europa or Ganymede.

references.label: NASA Science: Callisto

studiedBy.role: Orbited Jupiter until 2003; its data revealed the possible ocean.
Studied the moon on later passes.

notes.oneLine: Saturn's largest moon, with a thick atmosphere and rivers, lakes and seas of methane and ethane.

what.text: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon known to have a substantial atmosphere.

references.label: NASA Science: Titan

what.text: At the surface the pressure is about 60 percent greater than on Earth (atlas fact lists about 1.5 bar from Huygens; the NASA figure is slightly higher, both rounded).

references.label: NASA Science: Titan Facts

why.text: Titan is the only place besides Earth known to have liquids on its surface: clouds, rain, rivers, lakes and seas of liquid hydrocarbons such as methane and ethane.

references.label: NASA Science: Titan

discovery.text: Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan on 25 March 1655.

references.label: NASA Science: Titan Facts

uncertain.text: Titan is thought to have a subsurface ocean of water, suggested by radio signals recorded during the Huygens descent in 2005.

references.label: NASA Science: Titan Facts

uncertain.text: NASA says Titan's internal structure is not entirely known and scientists are not certain about its origin.

references.label: NASA Science: Titan Facts

studiedBy.role: Huygens probe descended to the surface in 2005; Cassini orbited Saturn 2004-2017.
Rotorcraft planned to launch in 2028 to make multiple landings over three years.
First spacecraft to explore Titan, passing through the Saturn system on 1 Sept 1979.

notes.oneLine: A small icy moon of Saturn whose south-polar jets are fed by an ocean inside it.

what.text: Enceladus is a small, icy world, about as wide as Arizona, with geyser-like jets that spew water vapour and ice particles into space.

references.label: NASA Science: Enceladus

what.text: NASA says it has the whitest, most reflective surface in the Solar System.

references.label: NASA Science: Enceladus

why.text: The jets come from relatively warm fractures in the crust called tiger stripes, and the south polar region is almost entirely free of impact craters.

references.label: NASA Science: Enceladus

why.text: Scientists determined that the jets are supplied by a global ocean inside the moon.

references.label: NASA Science: Enceladus

discovery.text: British astronomer William Herschel spotted Enceladus orbiting Saturn on 28 August 1789.

references.label: NASA Science: Enceladus

uncertain.text: Evidence points to hydrothermal vents deep beneath the icy shell, but this is inferred from plume data and has not been seen directly.

references.label: NASA Science: Enceladus

uncertain.text: Whether life could exist there is open; NASA calls Enceladus a 'promising lead' in the search for such worlds.

references.label: NASA Science: Enceladus

studiedBy.role: Observed the plumes and found the eruptions appear continuous, forming an enormous halo of fine ice dust.

notes.oneLine: Neptune's retrograde moon, thought to be a captured Kuiper Belt object, with active geysers.

what.text: Triton has a diameter of 2,700 km (atlas mean radius 1,352.6 km).

references.label: NASA Science: Triton

what.text: It consists of a crust of frozen nitrogen over an icy mantle believed to cover a core of rock and metal.

references.label: NASA Science: Triton

why.text: Triton is the only large moon in the Solar System that orbits in the opposite direction to its planet's rotation.

references.label: NASA Science: Triton

why.text: Voyager 2 found that Triton has active geysers.

references.label: NASA Science: Triton

discovery.text: Triton was discovered on 10 Oct 1846 by British astronomer William Lassell.

references.label: NASA Science: Triton

uncertain.text: Scientists think Triton is a Kuiper Belt object captured by Neptune's gravity; this is the leading hypothesis, not a confirmed fact.

references.label: NASA Science: Triton

studiedBy.role: The only spacecraft to fly past Neptune and Triton; photographed two-thirds of the moon and found it the coldest known planetary body in the Solar System.

notes.oneLine: Mars's larger moon, 27 by 22 by 18 km, orbiting Mars three times a day.

what.text: Phobos is the larger of Mars's two moons, about 27 by 22 by 18 km in size.

references.label: NASA Science: Phobos

what.text: It orbits Mars three times a day.

references.label: NASA Science: Phobos

why.text: Phobos was nearly shattered by a giant impact and has gouges from thousands of meteorite impacts.

references.label: NASA Science: Phobos

why.text: NASA says Phobos is on a collision course with Mars.

references.label: NASA Science: Phobos

discovery.text: Phobos was discovered on 17 Aug 1877 by Asaph Hall.

references.label: NASA Science: Phobos

uncertain.text: Phobos may be a captured asteroid, but some scientists have shown evidence that contradicts that theory.

references.label: NASA Science: Phobos

studiedBy.role: High-resolution camera imaging of Phobos.
Took images of Phobos's large crater.

notes.oneLine: Our own galaxy: a luminous barred spiral whose centre lies 8,178 pc from the Sun.

what.text: The Galaxy is a luminous (L-star) barred spiral with a central box/peanut bulge, a dominant disk and a diffuse stellar halo.

references.label: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, arXiv:1602.07702

what.text: The distance to the Galactic Centre black hole is R0 = 8178 +/- 13 (stat.) +/- 22 (sys.) pc, a geometric measurement (atlas: 8,178 pc, uncertainty 25.6 pc).

references.label: GRAVITY Collaboration 2019, arXiv:1904.05721

why.text: The Milky Way is a benchmark for understanding disk galaxies.

references.label: Bland-Hawthorn & Gerhard 2016, arXiv:1602.07702

uncertain.text: We view the Galaxy from inside, so its type is assigned partly by comparison with structural analogues: Kormendy and Bender class the Milky Way, NGC 4565 and NGC 5746 together as giant SBb-SBbc galaxies.

references.label: Kormendy & Bender 2019, arXiv:1810.10073

studiedBy.role: ESA mission charting the Galaxy in three dimensions: positions, distances and velocities of more than a billion stars; launched 19 Dec 2013.
Geometric distance to the Galactic Centre with 0.3% uncertainty.

notes.oneLine: Andromeda: a galaxy about 761 kpc (2.5 million light-years) away; Hubble's PHAT survey resolves its disk into stars.

what.text: Cepheid variables observed with Hubble give a distance to M31 of 761 +/- 11 kpc (distance modulus 24.407 +/- 0.032).
In angular size the galaxy is six times the apparent diameter of the full Moon.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 31

why.text: The Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury images about one third of M31's star-forming disk in six filters, aiming to resolve more than 100 million stars.

references.label: Dalcanton et al. 2012 (PHAT), arXiv:1204.0010

discovery.text: NASA says it is impossible to say who discovered the Andromeda Galaxy; the earliest known report is by the Persian astronomer al-Sufi in his Book of Fixed Stars (964).

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 31

uncertain.text: A 2012 Hubble study predicted a collision with the Milky Way in about four billion years, but a later editor's note says later Hubble and Gaia observations cast doubt on the certainty of that collision.

references.label: NASA Science: Hubble shows Milky Way destined for head-on collision with Andromeda (2012)

studiedBy.role: Treasury program imaging a third of the star-forming disk.
Near-infrared Cepheid period-luminosity distance anchored on LMC Cepheids.

notes.oneLine: The Triangulum Galaxy: a spiral about 840 kpc away, hosting the giant star-forming nebula NGC 604.

what.text: Hubble photometry of 154 Cepheids gives a distance to M33 of 840 +/- 11 kpc, a precision of about 1.3%.

references.label: Breuval et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.00037

what.text: NASA describes M33 as a spiral galaxy about half the size of the Milky Way and the third-largest galaxy in the Local Group; it rounds the distance to about 3 million light-years.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 33

why.text: NGC 604, in one of M33's spiral arms, is an enormous star-forming nebula nearly 1,500 light-years across.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 33

discovery.text: Charles Messier was the first to catalogue M33, observing it in August 1764; in the 1920s Edwin Hubble's study of its variable stars helped show it is a separate galaxy beyond our own.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 33

uncertain.text: The Cepheid calibration is anchored on Hubble observations of the Large Magellanic Cloud, so the M33 distance inherits that anchor's uncertainty.

references.label: Breuval et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.00037

studiedBy.role: Cepheid photometry for the distance; imaging of NGC 604.

notes.oneLine: The Large Magellanic Cloud: a companion galaxy 49.59 kpc away, home to the Tarantula Nebula.

what.text: Eclipsing binary stars give a distance to the LMC of 49.59 kpc with statistical and systematic uncertainties of 0.09 and 0.54 kpc, precise to 1%.

references.label: Pietrzynski et al. 2019, arXiv:1903.08096

what.text: NASA calls the LMC a companion galaxy of the Milky Way, with the Tarantula nebula at its heart.

references.label: NASA Hubble: Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud

why.text: The NGC 2070 cluster in the Tarantula nebula is a hotbed for young, massive stars.

references.label: NASA Hubble: Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud

uncertain.text: NASA's Hubble page rounds the distance to about 170,000 light-years (52,000 pc), which differs from the 49.59 kpc eclipsing-binary measurement used in the atlas.

references.label: NASA Hubble: Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud
Pietrzynski et al. 2019, arXiv:1903.08096

studiedBy.role: 20 eclipsing binaries gave the 1% distance (Pietrzynski et al. 2019).
Imaged the Tarantula Nebula and its star clusters.

reference.label: NASA Hubble: Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud

notes.oneLine: The Small Magellanic Cloud: centre at 62.44 kpc, and stretched along our line of sight.

what.text: Eclipsing binaries give a distance to the SMC centre of 62.44 +/- 0.47 (stat.) +/- 0.81 (syst.) kpc, an accuracy better than 2%.

references.label: Graczyk et al. 2020, arXiv:2010.08754

why.text: The targets form an elongated structure highly inclined to the plane of the sky, and the nearest and most distant systems differ by 10 kpc.

references.label: Graczyk et al. 2020, arXiv:2010.08754

uncertain.text: The authors find tentative evidence of a spherical stellar sub-structure (core) about 1.5 kpc in radial extent.

references.label: Graczyk et al. 2020, arXiv:2010.08754

studiedBy.role: Late-type eclipsing binaries used for the distance and 3D geometry (Graczyk et al. 2020).

notes.oneLine: M87: a giant elliptical galaxy whose central black hole was imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope.

what.text: M87 is an elliptical galaxy with several trillion stars and a supermassive black hole, and is the dominant member of the Virgo cluster.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 87

what.text: NASA gives about 54 million light-years (about 16.6 Mpc), matching the atlas distance of 16.67 Mpc.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 87

why.text: The Event Horizon Telescope imaged an asymmetric bright emission ring 42 +/- 3 micro-arcseconds across, consistent with the shadow of a Kerr black hole.

references.label: EHT Collaboration 2019, arXiv:1906.11238

why.text: A black-hole-powered jet of particles travels at nearly the speed of light.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 87

uncertain.text: The central mass of (6.5 +/- 0.7) x 10^9 solar masses comes from comparing the image to simulations, so it is a model-based inference.

references.label: EHT Collaboration 2019, arXiv:1906.11238

studiedBy.role: Radio-interferometric image of the black hole shadow, published 2019.
Imaged the galaxy, its jet and about 15,000 globular clusters (NASA estimate).

notes.oneLine: Centaurus A: a radio-loud galaxy with a dust lane, at about 3.8 Mpc.

what.text: Centaurus A is one of the foremost examples of a radio-loud active galactic nucleus, with a jet of high-energy particles seen in radio and X-ray images.

references.label: ESO: Radio galaxy Centaurus A (eso0005b)

what.text: Cepheids, tip-of-the-red-giant-branch, planetary-nebula, surface-brightness-fluctuation and Mira methods combine into a best-estimate distance of 3.8 +/- 0.1 Mpc.

references.label: Harris, Rejkuba & Harris 2009, arXiv:0911.3180

why.text: There is strong evidence that Centaurus A is a merger of an elliptical with a spiral galaxy; young blue stars lie along the edges of its dust lane.

references.label: ESO: Radio galaxy Centaurus A (eso0005b)

uncertain.text: ESO says the core probably contains a supermassive black hole of about 100 million solar masses; 'probably' marks this as an estimate.

references.label: ESO: Radio galaxy Centaurus A (eso0005b)

studiedBy.role: Optical imaging and the dust-lane and jet views on the ESO page.
Compared five high-precision distance methods on this galaxy.

notes.oneLine: Bode's Galaxy (M81): a spiral galaxy about 11.6 million light-years away with a 70-million-solar-mass black hole.

what.text: M81 is a spiral galaxy in Ursa Major whose spiral arms wind all the way down into its nucleus and are made up of young, hot, bluish stars.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 81

what.text: NASA gives 11.6 million light-years (about 3.56 Mpc); the atlas value is 3.60 Mpc.

references.label: NASA Hubble Messier 81
